title: Human Lung Anatomy: Lobes, Bronchi & Pleural Cavity Map
description: Explore human lung anatomy, including right and left lobes, the branching bronchial tree, pleural membranes, pulmonary vessels, and alveolar oxygen uptake.
h1: Human Lung Anatomy: Lobes, Bronchial Tree, Pleura and Gas Exchange
blurb: Twenty-three generations of branching airways lead to hundreds of millions of elastic alveoli where inspired air meets pulmonary capillary blood across 0.5 µm.
lead: Beneath the ribcage, two spongy, elastic lungs branch through more than twenty generations of airways to bring fresh air within a fraction of a micron of blood. In this illustrated guide to human lung anatomy, we examine 21 documented structures—including trachea, main & lobar bronchi, bronchioles, right lung — three lobes—linking regional topography, tissue architecture, physiological mechanisms, and clinical reasoning.
overview: Beneath the ribcage, two spongy, elastic lungs branch through more than twenty generations of airways to bring fresh air within a fraction of a micron of blood. Air is conducted from the trachea through progressively dividing bronchi and bronchioles until it reaches the alveoli, where oxygen diffuses into pulmonary capillaries and carbon dioxide diffuses out. The right lung has three lobes separated by oblique and horizontal fissures; the left has two, with a cardiac notch and lingula to accommodate the heart. Each lung is wrapped in visceral pleura, opposed by parietal pleura across a thin fluid-filled cavity whose surface tension keeps the lung expanded. Within the human body, the lungs (Pulmones) is situated in pleural cavities of the thorax, either side of the mediastinum, receives arterial perfusion via pulmonary arteries (gas exchange) + bronchial arteries (tissue supply), and is innervated by pulmonary plexus — vagus (bronchoconstriction) + sympathetic T2–T4.

The trachea is a 10–12 cm tube held open by 16–20 C-shaped hyaline cartilage rings, open posteriorly where the trachealis muscle lies. Lined by ciliated pseudostratified columnar epithelium with goblet cells. Physiologically, the trachea conducts, warms, humidifies and filters inspired air. The main & lobar bronchi (Bronchi principales et lobares) is the trachea divides at the carina (T4/T5) into right and left main bronchi, which divide into lobar then segmental bronchi. Cartilage plates replace rings as the airways narrow. Physiologically, the main & lobar bronchi governs distribute air to each lobe and bronchopulmonary segment. Structurally, the bronchioles (Bronchioli) comprises airways under 1 mm with no cartilage and relatively more smooth muscle, ending in terminal then respiratory bronchioles. Physiologically, the bronchioles regulate airflow resistance and deliver air to the alveolar ducts. The right lung — three lobes (Pulmo dexter) are superior, middle and inferior lobes separated by the oblique and horizontal fissures. Shorter than the left because the liver sits below, but wider and heavier. Physiologically, the right lung — three lobes governs gas exchange across ~150 million alveoli. The left lung — two lobes (Pulmo sinister) are superior and inferior lobes separated by the oblique fissure only. Narrower than the right because the heart bulges to the left. Physiologically, the left lung — two lobes governs gas exchange; the lingula of the superior lobe is the equivalent of the right middle lobe. The fissures (Fissurae pulmonis) are deep invaginations of visceral pleura. The oblique fissure runs in both lungs (T4 posteriorly to the 6th rib anteriorly); the horizontal fissure is right-sided only. Physiologically, the fissures allow the lobes to slide against each other and define surgical planes.

Clinically, regarding the trachea, foreign bodies more often enter the right main bronchus because it is wider, shorter and more vertical. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the main & lobar bronchi, each segmental bronchus supplies a bronchopulmonary segment that can be surgically removed on its own. In clinical pathology involving the bronchioles, smooth-muscle spasm of the bronchioles is the main problem in asthma; smooth muscle is also the target of salbutamol. Medical evaluation of the right lung — three lobes also notes that the right middle lobe is prone to collapse (middle-lobe syndrome) because its bronchus is narrow and surrounded by nodes.

questions.question: What are the lobes of the right and left lungs?
questions.answer: The right lung usually has superior, middle and inferior lobes; the left has superior and inferior lobes with a cardiac notch. Fissures divide the lobes, though normal anatomy can vary.

questions.question: Where does air go after the bronchi?
questions.answer: Air passes from the bronchi into bronchioles and then through the respiratory zone to the alveoli, where gas exchange occurs.

questions.question: What is a Type I pneumocyte?
questions.answer: A Type I pneumocyte is a very thin squamous cell forming much of the alveolar gas-exchange surface. It can be recognized on the separate microscopic-scale teaching illustration, not on the whole-lung image.

questions.question: What does a Type II pneumocyte do?
questions.answer: A Type II pneumocyte is a plumper alveolar cell that secretes pulmonary surfactant, which helps reduce surface tension. It also contributes to maintenance and repair of the alveolar lining.

questions.question: Is the enlarged alveolar image an actual microscope slide?
questions.answer: No. It is a digital educational illustration showing the relationship of alveolar lining cells to the air space, not a microscope slide or literal magnification.
